topic: Dandelin Spheres: The Geometric Magic of Conic Sections
target_audience: Advanced High School or First-Year University Mathematics Students

sections.title: The Mystery of the Slice
sections.content: Introduce the concept of a right circular cone being intersected by a plane. While we know these intersections create ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas, the 'why' is often missing. This section defines the goal: proving that the intersection curve is an ellipse using a beautiful 3D construction.
sections.example: A wizard character, 'Mathemagician Max', uses a laser-thin sword to slice through a glowing ice-cream cone at an angle, revealing a perfect oval (ellipse) glowing on the surface.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The 'Equal Tangent' Rule
sections.content: Establish a critical geometric foundation: From any single point outside a sphere, the lengths of the two tangent segments to the sphere are exactly equal. This is the 'secret weapon' for the upcoming proof.
sections.example: An animation of a squirrel standing at a point P outside a giant snowball. It holds two straight sticks that just touch the snowball at points A and B. A measuring tape shows that PA = PB regardless of where the squirrel moves the sticks.

sections.title: Summoning the Dandelin Spheres
sections.content: Introduce the construction: Place two spheres (Dandelin Spheres) inside the cone. One is small and sits above the intersecting plane; the other is large and sits below. Each sphere must be tangent to the cone (along a circle) and tangent to the plane (at a single point). Let these points of tangency on the plane be F1 and F2.
sections.example: Visualize two soap bubbles inflating inside a funnel until they are snugly 'wedged' between the funnel walls and a tilted glass sheet. The points where the bubbles touch the glass are highlighted as 'Magic Foci' (F1 and F2).

sections.title: The Step-by-Step Proof
sections.content: Pick an arbitrary point P on the intersection curve. Using the tangent rule from Section 2, show that the distance from P to F1 is equal to the distance from P to the upper circle of tangency on the cone. Similarly, PF2 equals the distance to the lower circle. Therefore, PF1 + PF2 equals the slant distance between the two circles, which is constant.
sections.example: A glowing string is drawn from F1 to P and then to F2. As P slides around the edge of the slice, the animation shows the segments mapping onto the side of the cone, maintaining a constant total length, satisfying the definition of an ellipse.

sections.title: Generalization and Real-World Echoes
sections.content: Explain that this logic isn't just for ellipses. By changing the angle of the plane, Dandelin spheres can also define parabolas and hyperbolas. Conclude with why this matters: it links 3D spatial geometry with 2D coordinate geometry.
sections.example: A 'Section-O-Matic' machine shifts the plane's angle. We see the Dandelin spheres resize and shift to stay tangent, showing how the math holds true for a satellite's orbit (ellipse) or a comet's flyby (hyperbola).
